purpose: Precisely test correct and incorrect answer variants for 14 unpatched, genuine first-school-mock AQA AS Physics/Chemistry original short recall cards, with no duplicate cards.
scope: Seven Physics cards covering plots, spring constant, projectiles, ionisation limit and zero error; seven Chemistry cards covering equilibrium, calorimetry, kinetics, successive ionisation energies, bond fission and back titrations.
source: deck.json original core, 3345 unchanged IDs; app.js production answer evaluator and mock filter
safeguards: Apply only if id, subject, AS stage, mock=true and complete original front/back match.
Retain existing accepted responses and save keys; do not change original model answer, question, stage or mock scope.
Run all 14 original model answers, 14 new acceptable paraphrases, 28 misconception probes through real evaluateCard.
Do not mistake precision on these selected cards for whole AQA syllabus coverage, or automated marking for manual drawing or calculation checking.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why use a best-fit line rather than joining points dot-to-dot?
rows.originalBack: A best-fit line reveals the overall relationship and reduces the influence of random scatter.
accept: A best-fit line follows the overall trend rather than each scattered point, limiting the effect of random errors.
reject: Join every point individually, since a zigzag line removes random scatter.
The best-fit line must always pass through every measured point.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: How do areas under force–time and force–displacement graphs differ?
rows.originalBack: Force–time area = impulse Δp; force–displacement area = work done W.
accept: Area under force against time equals impulse or change in momentum; area under force against displacement equals work done.
reject: Force-time area gives work, while force-displacement area gives impulse.
Area under either graph always gives velocity rather than work or momentum change.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: For an ohmic conductor, what is the gradient of V against I versus I against V?
rows.originalBack: V (y) vs I (x): gradient = R. I (y) vs V (x): gradient = 1/R.
accept: The gradient of V plotted against I is resistance R, whereas the gradient of I against V is 1/R.
reject: The gradient of V against I is 1/R and that of I against V is R.
Both graph gradients equal the resistance in ohms.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: A projectile returns to its launch height. Which component fixes the flight time, and which fixes range once time is known?
rows.originalBack: Vertical initial velocity and gravity fix flight time. Horizontal initial velocity × flight time gives range.
accept: The vertical component with gravity determines time of flight; horizontal speed multiplied by this time gives range.
reject: Horizontal velocity alone decides the flight time; vertical velocity decides range.
Only vertical speed matters for horizontal range, even if horizontal velocity is zero.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalBack: Force divided by extension within the linear region.
accept: For a linear spring k=F/x, the load divided by its extension.
reject: Spring constant is extension divided by force, x/F.
The spring constant is the area under a force-extension graph.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What does 0 eV mean on an atomic energy-level diagram?
rows.originalBack: The ionisation limit: the electron is free. Bound levels have negative energies.
accept: Zero electron energy is the ionisation threshold, when the electron is unbound; bound levels are negative.
reject: Zero eV is the lowest bound ground-state energy and an ionised electron must be negative.
Bound atomic electron levels have positive energies relative to the free-electron limit.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalBack: A systematic offset when the true input is zero.
accept: A zero error is an instrument's systematic non-zero indication when the true quantity is zero.
reject: A zero error is the random variation between repeated readings.
A zero error means the instrument always reads exactly zero for a genuine zero input.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How can equilibrium composition change without changing Kc?
rows.originalBack: Concentration or pressure changes can shift equilibrium; Kc remains constant at unchanged temperature.
accept: At fixed temperature changing concentration or pressure can alter equilibrium composition, but Kc stays unchanged.
reject: Increasing reactant concentration increases the numerical value of Kc at the same temperature.
Increasing gas pressure always increases the equilibrium constant Kc.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: In q = mcΔT, what mass normally appears?
rows.originalBack: Mass of the substance whose temperature change is measured.
accept: In q=mcΔT, m is the mass of the material whose temperature change was measured.
reject: The m in q=mcΔT is always the number of moles of limiting reagent.
Use the mass of the reacting metal even when only the solution's temperature change was recorded.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is one frequent source of error in simple calorimetry?
accept: Unwanted heat transfer to or from the surroundings causes inaccuracy in calorimetry.
reject: Calorimetry never loses heat to the surroundings if any cup is used.
Heat exchange with the surroundings has no effect on measured temperature changes.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Why does heating increase reaction rate disproportionately?
rows.originalBack: A larger fraction of particles exceed activation energy.
accept: Higher temperature means a much larger fraction of colliding particles has energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.
reject: Heating an uncatalysed mixture lowers the reaction's activation energy.
Heating increases the rate solely because the activation energy becomes zero.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What causes a large jump between successive ionisation energies?
rows.originalBack: The next electron is removed from an inner shell.
accept: A large successive-ionisation-energy jump occurs when the next electron is taken from an inner shell closer to the nucleus.
reject: The jump shows the next electron must be from a more distant outer shell.
The electron after the jump is held less strongly because the shielding is greater.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: How is homolytic fission different from heterolytic fission?
rows.originalBack: Homolytic splits the pair; heterolytic transfers both electrons to one side.
accept: Homolytic fission divides the bonding pair one electron to each atom; heterolytic fission gives both to one atom.
reject: Homolytic fission gives both bonding electrons to one atom; heterolytic gives one to each.
Both homolytic and heterolytic bond breaking always produce two radicals.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: State the essential subtraction in a back titration.
rows.originalBack: Initial moles of reagent minus remaining moles = moles that reacted.
accept: Moles of excess reagent that reacted equal moles initially added minus moles left over.
reject: Add the initial and remaining reagent moles to calculate the amount consumed.
All initially added excess reagent is counted as reacted, even when some is left over.
